The definition of an ellipse uses distances between points in a plane, so first learn to calculate distances.
An ellipse can be viewed as a circle stretched in one direction, so the circle equation provides a comparison.
When studying an ellipse with coordinates, plane-line equations are the basis for finding intersections.
The standard ellipse equation is derived from the constant-sum-of-distances definition.
The relation a²=b²+c² among a, b, and c is a parameter relation in the standard equation.
The range, symmetry, and vertices can all be read from the standard equation.
Simple applications require using the ellipse's vertices and parameters a, b, and c.
The hyperbola definition replaces the ellipse's sum of distances with the absolute difference of distances.
The standard hyperbola equation follows from the constant-difference-of-distances definition.
The standard form resembles the ellipse equation, but the signs and relation between a and b differ.
The vertices, range, and symmetry of a hyperbola can be read from its standard equation.
The asymptote equations are determined by the standard hyperbola equation.
A parabola also uses a distance definition, with distance to a focus on one side and distance to a directrix on the other.
Distance to a directrix is distance to a line.
The standard parabola equation is derived from the focus-directrix definition.
The vertex, axis of symmetry, and opening direction can be read from the standard equation.
Simple parabola applications require using its standard equation and focus.
Finding the number of intersections after substituting a line into an ellipse equation requires the ellipse equation first.
Write the line in a form that can be substituted; either general or slope-intercept form works.
A sequence is a function defined on the positive integers, so first learn the concept of a function.
Listing terms, giving a general term, and drawing a graph are all ways to represent the same sequence.
The index n in a general term has a range, just as a function has a domain.
Finding a specific term from the general term requires knowing that it is one representation of a sequence.
A simple recurrence defines a term from the previous one, so first distinguish each term's index.
An arithmetic sequence is a special sequence whose consecutive terms differ by a constant.
The general term a_n=a_1+(n−1)d follows directly from the definition of an arithmetic sequence.
The arithmetic-sequence formula is still a general term, so first learn to substitute an index into it.
The arithmetic mean follows from the relationship between neighboring terms and uses the same common difference as the general term.
The sum of the first n terms is derived by adding the terms in order or in reverse order.
Viewing a_n as a linear function of n requires knowing the general term first.
Practical arithmetic-sequence problems usually require both the general term and the sum.
A geometric sequence is a special sequence whose consecutive-term ratio is constant.
The general term a_n=a_1 q^(n−1) follows from the definition of a geometric sequence.
Substituting an index to find a term is still an application of the general-term formula.
A geometric mean satisfies a square relationship that follows from the constant common ratio.
The sum of the first n terms follows from the geometric-series formula for the terms.
Viewing the general term as an exponential function requires knowing the geometric-sequence formula first.
A geometric sequence and an exponential function have the same kind of growth, but one has a discrete domain and the other a continuous one.
Problems about repeated growth or decay use the geometric general term or sum.
Mathematical induction concerns propositions about positive integers, with recurrence as a direct motivating example.
Induction proves propositions, so first learn what a proposition and a proof are.
To prove a statement by induction, first learn to write the base case and inductive step.
Early textbook examples of induction often prove identities such as the arithmetic-sequence general term.
Average rate of change compares how function values change with the independent variable, so first learn monotonicity.
Instantaneous rate is the limit of average rates as the increment approaches zero, so first learn to calculate average rates.
A derivative is the instantaneous rate of change at a point, and its definition uses limits.
Treating the derivative at each point as a function of the independent variable gives the derivative function.
The geometric meaning of a derivative is the tangent slope; its value is still the derivative at that point.
A tangent slope is a line slope, already introduced with line equations and angles of inclination.
Writing a tangent equation requires knowing that its slope equals the derivative at the point of tangency.
Once the point of tangency and slope are known, write the tangent in point-slope form.
Basic derivative formulas come from calculations using the derivative definition.
Power-function derivatives are among the first basic formulas derived from the definition.
The differentiation rules for arithmetic operations combine basic derivatives to handle more complex functions.
The derivative of f(ax+b) is the simplest chain-rule case, so first learn the basic differentiation rules.
This simple composition is used when exponential, logarithmic, or similar functions contain ax+b.
Using derivatives to determine monotonicity requires being able to find the derivative first.
Finding intervals of monotonicity means solving inequalities where the derivative is positive or negative.
Extrema occur where monotonicity changes; both necessary and sufficient conditions follow from this.
Finding extrema on a closed interval requires comparing endpoint values with interior extrema.
Maximum and minimum values were defined among function properties; derivatives provide a method for finding them.
Maximizing profit or minimizing materials turns an applied problem into finding an extreme value on an open or closed interval.
For polynomials of degree at most three, monotonic intervals are determined by the derivative, a polynomial of degree at most two.
For these polynomials, use derivative signs and endpoint values together to find extrema and closed-interval maximum or minimum values.
The addition principle extends the simple arrangements learned in elementary school.
Listing mutually exclusive cases and counting them is a concrete use of the addition principle.
The multiplication principle is often used with the addition principle, so first distinguish when to add.
For combined counting, first identify the steps to multiply, then handle the cases within them.
The number of permutations comes from choosing each position in successive steps; different orders count separately.
The permutation formula is the counting result of the permutation definition.
Use permutations for queues and assigning distinct roles, not just for selecting people.
The difference between combinations and permutations is whether order matters, so first learn that permutations count order.
The combination formula is obtained by dividing the permutation count by the orderings within each group.
A combination count equals a permutation count divided by k factorial, so first learn to calculate permutations.
Symmetry and the addition identity are both properties of combination numbers.
Use combinations directly for selections and samples where order does not matter.
Binomial coefficients are combination numbers; each term in the expansion uses C(n,k).
A specified term and its coefficient are read from the general term of the binomial theorem.
Setting a=b=1 in the theorem gives the sum of all binomial coefficients.
Coefficient symmetry follows from the combination identity C(n,k)=C(n,n−k).
Each row of Pascal's triangle is a row of binomial coefficients, and its sum is 2 to the power n.
Calculating conditional probability among equally likely outcomes requires the classical probability model.
The multiplication rule expresses a joint event as the probability of one event times a conditional probability.
Multiplying probabilities of independent events is a special case where the conditional probability equals the event's own probability.
The total probability rule adds path probabilities across causes, using the multiplication rule within each cause.
The denominator in Bayes' formula is the total probability of the observed outcome.
Recognizing independence by checking whether P(B|A) equals P(B) requires conditional probability first.
This restates the required-course idea of independence using conditional-probability language.
A random variable assigns a real number to each sample point, so first learn sample spaces.
Calculating probabilities from a distribution later still uses multiplication for joint events.
A distribution lists the probability of each value of a discrete random variable.
A two-point distribution is a distribution with values 0 and 1 only.
The mean is a weighted sum of values and probabilities from the distribution.
The mean is a probability-weighted average, so first learn the meaning of an average.
Variance is defined using squared deviations from the mean, so calculate the mean first.
Variance of a random variable and sample variance both measure dispersion.
The outcome of one Bernoulli trial can be represented by a two-point distribution.
A binomial distribution records the number of successes in n Bernoulli trials.
The probability of a given number of successes contains a combination number, the same value as a binomial coefficient.
For a binomial distribution, np is the mean and np(1−p) is the variance.
These formulas are the mean and variance specialized to a binomial distribution.
Without-replacement probabilities use combination numbers for both the numerator and denominator.
A hypergeometric distribution also lists a probability for each possible value.
The mean nK/N applies specifically to the hypergeometric distribution.
It is still a closed-form formula for the mean of a distribution.
The shape of a normal curve can be seen in the outline of a frequency histogram.
The axis of symmetry of a normal curve is its mean.
The empirical rule describes the proportion of a normal curve within several standard deviations of the mean.
Before examining paired data, learn to describe a data set using sample statistics.
The correlation coefficient quantifies the linear trend shown in a scatterplot.
Comparing correlation strength means comparing the absolute values of sample correlation coefficients.
Fit a straight line only after identifying a linear relationship.
A regression line is based on a linear function.
Least squares selects specific parameters for this line with random error.
The slope and intercept formulas are estimates derived from the least-squares principle.
Deriving the slope involves sums of squared terms, with quadratic equations providing the algebraic background.
Substitute a new x into the estimated line to obtain a prediction.
Each cell in a contingency table is a category frequency; frequencies and relative frequencies were introduced in the required course.
Row and column totals are found by adding mutually exclusive cells.
The independence test measures how far this contingency table departs from the independence assumption.
Independence here is the same idea as independence of events, applied to categorical variables.
The statistic turns the departure measured by the independence test into a number.
A key step in statistical modeling and prediction is making a prediction with the regression line and then checking it.
Statistical modeling in the same volume also considers whether categorical variables are associated.
